standard.title: The Women's Movement
standard.description: the significant events, individuals and groups in the women's movement in Australia, and how they have changed the role and status of women
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined women's wartime roles and the change-versus-continuity pattern in K04 — including that most wartime gains were reversed post-war. They have studied suffrage from earlier year levels. They have not yet examined the post-1945 women's movement as a sustained organised campaign, the specific legal changes that followed, or the ongoing gap between formal equality and lived experience.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate significant events, individuals and groups in the Australian women's movement and evaluate how they changed the role and status of women.

nodes.label: The post-war domestic settlement and its limits
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the post-war domestic settlement — the social and economic pressures that returned women to domestic roles — and why this settlement produced the conditions for organised feminist activism.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two features of the post-war domestic settlement; explain how each created conditions that motivated feminist activism.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the post-war return to domesticity — government incentives, social messaging, industrial restructuring that removed women from wartime roles; explain the 'marriage bar' as a concrete legislative mechanism (women required to resign from public service upon marriage); examine the gap between formal citizenship equality and the lived reality of employment and legal discrimination; explain how this gap — experienced by educated women in particular — motivated the second-wave feminist movement of the 1960s–70s.
wider: Examine The Female Eunuch (1970) and The Feminine Mystique (1963) as texts that named the post-war domestic settlement as a problem — analysing how intellectual frameworks shaped the women's movement
Compare Australia's post-war domestic settlement with Britain's or the USA's — examining whether the scale and character of the feminist response differed and why
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the post-war domestic settlement — specifically the marriage bar and employment discrimination as concrete mechanisms, not just general sexism — is the prerequisite for understanding what the women's movement was campaigning against. Students who lack this context cannot explain why specific campaigns targeted specific changes.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat the women's movement as a response to general inequality without examining the specific structural mechanisms that made activism necessary. Making the marriage bar, employment law, and social pressure explicit — as mechanisms, not just attitudes — provides the concrete targets that explain why particular campaigns emerged when they did.

success_criteria: Describes at least two features of the post-war domestic settlement — including the marriage bar as a specific mechanism
Explains the gap between formal citizenship equality and lived employment/legal reality
Explains how this gap motivated organised feminist activism

nodes.label: Key events and campaigns — legal and workplace change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain significant events connected to women's rights in the workforce since 1945, including the repeal of the marriage bar, equal pay campaigns, and the Sex Discrimination Act.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least three events or campaigns connected to women's workforce rights and evaluate what each changed.
nodes.typical_width: Students trace key events: the 1966 repeal of the marriage bar in the Commonwealth Public Service; the equal pay case (1969 and 1972 ACTU cases); the introduction of maternity leave; the Sex Discrimination Act 1984; the changing nature of women's participation in employment from the 1960s to present; the persistence of the gender pay gap despite formal equality legislation; explain how each change was achieved — who campaigned, through what means, and what opposition was faced.
wider: Examine the equal pay cases in depth — analysing the arguments made, the industrial tribunal's reasoning, and why equal pay in principle has not produced equal pay in practice

Investigate the gender pay gap today — using current data to evaluate whether the legislative changes of the 1970s–80s have produced genuine workforce equality, and what structural factors maintain the gap
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The gap between formal legislative equality and the persistent gender pay gap is a rich analytical question that connects historical change to present-day data — students can evaluate whether the movement's legal achievements translated into structural equality.

response_modes.reason: Students need a working knowledge of the key legislative and workplace milestones before evaluation of the movement's overall impact is meaningful. Building the repertoire systematically prevents the reductive focus on one or two famous events.

success_criteria: Explains at least three events or campaigns connected to women's workforce rights
Evaluates what each change produced — not merely describes it
Identifies at least one way formal legal change has not produced full practical equality

nodes.label: Significant individuals and their contributions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the contributions of significant individuals in the women's movement, evaluating how their contributions advanced the movement.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the contributions of at least two significant individuals across different domains (political, activist, cultural) and evaluate each.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine contributions across domains: political leaders (Gough Whitlam government's women's policy agenda, Joan Child as first female Speaker); activists and organisers (Women's Electoral Lobby, women's refuges movement); cultural contributors (Germaine Greer, Dale Spender); legal reformers; explain what each contributed, through what means, and what opposition they faced; apply the K10 evaluation framework — what type of change, how durable, how broad.
wider: Examine the contributions of significant Indigenous women leaders — analysing how their work navigated both gender and racial discrimination, and how their contributions have been recognised relative to non-Indigenous women leaders
Investigate the role of men who supported women's rights — examining what motivated male allies, what they contributed, and how their involvement affected the movement's direction

response_modes.reason: Examining individuals across political, activist, and cultural domains gives a fuller picture than focusing on political leaders alone. The movement operated across multiple spheres simultaneously; covering multiple domains reflects this.

success_criteria: Explains the contributions of at least two individuals across different domains
Applies the evaluation framework to assess the impact of each contribution
Identifies at least one contribution from outside formal politics

nodes.label: How the women's movement changed roles and status — evaluation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate how the women's movement changed the role and status of women in Australia, identifying what changed, what limits remain, and what ongoing campaigns address.
nodes.minimum_width: Students construct an evaluative claim about how the women's movement changed roles and status, identifying at least two changes and at least one significant limit.
nodes.typical_width: Students draw on N1–N3 to evaluate change across domains — workforce participation, legal rights, political representation, cultural attitudes; identify what changed durably, what changed formally but not practically (gender pay gap, domestic violence rates), and what remains contested; connect to K13's content on continuing struggles; evaluate whether the movement's achievements represent a transformation or an incremental improvement in women's status.
wider: Evaluate the contemporary #MeToo movement as a continuation of the women's movement — analysing what it achieved, what it revealed about the limits of earlier legislative change, and how social media changed the dynamics of feminist activism
Compare women's status in Australia with another comparable country — evaluating whether Australia's women's movement produced more or less change than comparable societies
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The #MeToo comparison and the cross-country evaluation connect historical study to present-day questions — students can evaluate whether the movement's achievements have been sufficient and what ongoing activism reveals about remaining structural inequality.

response_modes.reason: This node draws together the context (N1), legislative and workplace changes (N2), and individual contributions (N3) into an overall evaluation. Tasks requiring students to argue about the extent and limits of change across multiple domains work well here.

success_criteria: Evaluates how the women's movement changed roles and status — identifying at least two durable changes
Identifies at least one significant area where formal change has not produced practical equality
Connects the historical movement to ongoing campaigns, explaining the continuity
